title: Daedalus et Icarus. Perdix
titleEn: Daedalus, Icarus and Perdix — Metamorphoses VIII.183–259
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Daedalus, sick of Crete and of his long exile and shut in by the sea, makes wings out of feathers, thread and wax, warns his son Icarus to fly a middle path between the water that would weigh the feathers down and the fire that would burn them, and takes off with him; the boy begins to enjoy the flight, climbs higher than he was told to, and falls into water that is called after him. The father buries him and curses his own craft. At the graveside a partridge claps its wings and sings — his sister's son, whom Daedalus once threw headlong from Minerva's citadel out of envy, and whom Pallas caught in mid-air and made into a bird that will not go high.

sentences.t:
Daedalus interea Creten longumque perosus
exsilium tactusque loci natalis amore
clausus erat pelago.
sentences.l: Daedalus meanwhile, having come to loathe Crete and his long exile, and touched by love of his native place, was shut in by the sea.
sentences.i: Daedalus, meanwhile, had come to hate Crete and his long exile, and love of the place he was born in had touched him; but the sea shut him in.
sentences.n: perosus is the perfect participle of perodi, “to detest”, and it is active in meaning — Daedalus hates, he is not hated — and it governs the two accusatives Creten and exsilium. Creten keeps the Greek accusative ending, which the poem uses freely for Greek names. tactus, by contrast, really is passive: the love does the touching. clausus erat pelago: the ablative is the barrier that shuts him in, not a person doing the shutting.

sentences.t:
“Terras licet” inquit “et undas
obstruat: at caelum certe patet; ibimus illac.
Omnia possideat, non possidet aera Minos.”
sentences.l: “Though he block the lands,” he says, “and the waves — yet the sky at least lies open; that way we shall go. Let him own all things: Minos does not own the air.”
sentences.i: “Let him block the land,” he said, “and block the sea — the sky at any rate is open, and that is the way we go. Let Minos own everything; the air he does not own.”
sentences.n: licet with the subjunctive obstruat is concessive, “granted that he blocks”, and possideat in the last line is a jussive subjunctive doing the same work, “let him own”. The last line is one verb used twice, subjunctive against indicative: the concession granted and then taken straight back. The subject Minos is held to the very end, so the reader hears “does not own the air” before hearing whose air is meant. Magnus prints at caelum, “but the sky”; some editions print et, which joins the clause instead of setting it against what came before.

sentences.t:
Dixit et ignotas animum dimittit in artes
naturamque novat.
sentences.l: He spoke, and sends his mind off into arts unknown, and makes nature new.
sentences.i: He said it, and turned his mind loose on arts nobody knew, and made nature over.
sentences.n: The perfect dixit and the presents dimittit and novat stand side by side: the speech is finished and done with, the making begins and is happening now. This alternation of perfect with historic present runs the whole length of the flight and is worth watching for. ignotas … in artes is split around animum, so the mind is inside the unknown before we are told what it is inside. naturam novat is as blunt as it sounds: novo is “to make new”, and two words do the whole of it.

sentences.t:
Nam ponit in ordine pennas,
a minima coeptas, longam breviore sequenti,
ut clivo crevisse putes.
sentences.l: For he lays feathers in a row, begun from the smallest, a long one with a shorter one following, so that you would think they had grown on a slope.
sentences.i: He laid feathers out in order, beginning from the smallest, a long one with a shorter one after it — you would think the whole thing had grown up a hillside.
sentences.n: coeptas is a perfect participle agreeing with pennas, “begun from the smallest”. longam breviore sequenti is the compressed part: breviore sequenti is an ablative absolute with longam as the object of sequenti, “with a shorter one following a long one”. Taken together with a minima coeptas the two halves point in opposite directions along the wing, and the Latin does not settle which end is which; what is certain, and what the pipe in the next lines confirms, is that the feathers are graded and unequal. putes is a potential subjunctive with an indefinite “you”, “you would think”; clivo is an ablative of place, “on a slope”.

sentences.t:
Sic rustica quondam
fistula disparibus paulatim surgit avenis.
sentences.l: Just so the rustic pipe at times rises little by little with unequal reeds.
sentences.i: It is the way a shepherd's pipe climbs by degrees on reeds that are not the same length.
sentences.n: quondam in a simile is not “once, formerly” but “sometimes, as at times”: the comparison is to a thing that happens, not to a thing that happened. fistula is the pan-pipe, and avena is literally an oat-straw, the material a reed pipe is made of. surgit, “rises”, sees the pipe as a stepped slope, which is what clivo in the line before had already made of the wing.

sentences.t:
Tum lino medias et ceris adligat imas,
atque ita compositas parvo curvamine flectit,
ut veras imitetur aves.
sentences.l: Then with thread he binds the middle ones, and with wax the lowest, and, so arranged, bends them with a small curve, so that it may imitate true birds.
sentences.i: Then he tied the middle feathers with thread and the bottom ones with wax, and once they were set in place he gave them a slight curve, so that the thing came out like real birds.
sentences.n: medias and imas are feminine accusative plurals with pennas understood from the line before: the middle feathers and the lowest. The two fastenings are the point of the line — thread in the middle, wax at the base — and it is the wax that gives way later in this part. veras aves is emphatic by position: what he is copying is not wings but birds.

sentences.t:
Puer Icarus una
stabat et, ignarus sua se tractare pericla,
ore renidenti modo, quas vaga moverat aura,
captabat plumas,
sentences.l: The boy Icarus stood alongside, and, not knowing that he was handling his own dangers, with a beaming face now kept snatching at the feathers that the roving breeze had stirred,
sentences.i: The boy Icarus stood there beside him, with no idea that what he was handling was his own danger, and with his face bright he kept snatching at feathers a stray breeze had stirred,
sentences.n: ignarus takes an accusative and infinitive: se tractare, “that he was handling”, with sua pericla as the object of tractare. Both reflexives, sua and se, point at the boy, so the line says twice over whose danger it is. The relative clause quas vaga moverat aura comes before its antecedent plumas, which is ordinary in verse and worth getting used to. renidenti is the present participle of renideo, “to shine, to beam”, used of a face.

sentences.t:
flavam modo pollice ceram
mollibat lusuque suo mirabile patris
impediebat opus.
sentences.l: now with his thumb kept softening the yellow wax, and with his own play kept getting in the way of his father's marvellous work.
sentences.i: and now worked the yellow wax soft under his thumb, and with his playing got in the way of the marvel his father was making.
sentences.n: mollibat is a syncopated form of molliebat, imperfect; the shorter form is metrically convenient and common in verse. The three imperfects here — captabat, mollibat, impediebat — hold the boy in continuous play while the work goes forward around him, and the play is all the poem lets us see him do. mirabile is set apart from its noun opus at the line's end, so the wonder is named before the thing that is wonderful. The wax he is softening with his thumb is the wax that holds the wing together.

sentences.t:
Postquam manus ultima coepto
imposita est, geminas opifex libravit in alas
ipse suum corpus motaque pependit in aura.
sentences.l: After the last hand was laid on the thing begun, the maker balanced his own body on the twin wings and hung in the air he had set moving.
sentences.i: When the last touch had been given to what he had begun, the maker poised his own body on the two wings and hung there on the air his beating stirred.
sentences.n: manus ultima imponere is a set phrase for finishing a piece of work — putting the last hand to it. coepto is a neuter participle used as a noun, “the thing begun”, in the dative. opifex, “maker, workman”, is the word the poem uses for Daedalus here in place of his name. mota in aura is the air his own wings have set moving: the first flight is held up by the beat that made it.

sentences.t:
Instruit et natum “medio” que “ut limite curras,
Icare,” ait “moneo, ne, si demissior ibis,
unda gravet pennas, si celsior, ignis adurat.
sentences.l: He instructs his son as well: “I warn you, Icarus,” he says, “to run by a middle path — for fear that, if you go too low, the wave should weigh the feathers down; if too high, the fire should scorch them.”
sentences.i: He gave his son his instructions too. “Keep to a middle path, Icarus,” he said. “That is my warning. Go too low and the water will weigh your feathers down; too high, and the fire will burn them.”
sentences.n: moneo with ut and the subjunctive curras is the ordinary construction, “I warn you to run”. limes is a track or a boundary-line, so the middle way is drawn as a marked lane with an edge on either side. demissior and celsior are comparatives used absolutely — lower than you should go, higher than you should go — not comparisons with anything named. gravet and adurat are subjunctives in the ne-clause depending on moneo. The two dangers are named low first and high second, which is not the order the flight will take: it is the high one that undoes him, and the water below only receives what the sun has already ruined.

sentences.t:
Inter utrumque vola. Nec te spectare Booten
aut Helicen iubeo strictumque Orionis ensem:
me duce carpe viam.”
sentences.l: Fly between the two. Nor do I bid you look at Boötes or Helice, or the drawn sword of Orion: with me leading, take the road.”
sentences.i: Fly between them. And I am not telling you to watch for Boötes, or Helice, or Orion's drawn sword: I will lead, and you take the road.”
sentences.n: inter utrumque vola says in three words what the warning has just said at length: the same order twice, once explained and once bare. Boötes the Ox-driver, Helice the Great Bear and the drawn sword of Orion are the marks a sailor steers by, so the instruction is not to navigate but to follow. me duce is the two-noun ablative absolute — “with me as leader” — which has no participle because sum has no present participle; the phrase comes back at line 224, where the boy leaves his ducem behind.

sentences.t:
Pariter praecepta volandi
tradit et ignotas umeris accommodat alas.
sentences.l: At the same time he hands over the rules of flying and fits the unknown wings to his shoulders.
sentences.i: As he spoke he was passing on the rules of flight and fitting the strange wings to the boy's shoulders.
sentences.n: volandi is a gerund in the genitive depending on praecepta, “instructions of flying”. ignotas repeats the word used of the arts at line 188: the wings are unknown in the same way the craft was unknown, and the repetition is deliberate. umeris is dative after accommodat.

sentences.t:
Inter opus monitusque genae maduere seniles,
et patriae tremuere manus.
sentences.l: Between the work and the warnings the old cheeks grew wet, and a father's hands trembled.
sentences.i: Between the working and the warning the old man's cheeks went wet, and a father's hands shook.
sentences.n: maduere and tremuere are the poetic third person plural perfect in -ēre, the same as maduerunt and tremuerunt; the shorter ending is very common in verse and will keep appearing. Both adjectives do work an English genitive would do: genae seniles, “the old cheeks”, means the old man's, and patriae manus, “fatherly hands”, means the father's. The poem calls him old and calls him father in one line and uses his name in neither.

sentences.t:
Dedit oscula nato
non iterum repetenda suo, pennisque levatus
ante volat comitique timet, velut ales, ab alto
quae teneram prolem produxit in aera nido,
sentences.l: He gave kisses to his son, kisses not to be repeated a second time, and, lifted on his feathers, he flies in front and fears for his companion, like a bird that has led its tender brood out into the air from a high nest,
sentences.i: He kissed his son — kisses that would never be repeated — and, lifted on his feathers, he flew ahead, afraid for the companion behind him, like a bird that has brought her soft brood out of a high nest into the air,
sentences.n: repetenda is a gerundive agreeing with oscula and carries the whole line: the kisses are “not to be repeated”, and the poem says so before anything has gone wrong. levatus is a perfect participle used of himself rising on the wings. comiti is dative after timet, “he fears for his companion”, and comes, the partner on a journey, is the word the poem chooses here for his son. In the simile ales is picked up by the feminine quae, so the parent bird is a mother where the parent in the story is a father.

sentences.t:
hortaturque sequi damnosasque erudit artes
et movet ipse suas et nati respicit alas.
sentences.l: and he urges him to follow and teaches him the ruinous arts, and himself moves his own wings and looks back at his son's.
sentences.i: and he urged the boy to follow, and taught him the arts that would ruin him, and moved his own wings, and kept looking back at his son's.
sentences.n: hortatur is a deponent — passive in form, active in meaning, “he urges”. damnosas, “causing loss, ruinous”, is the poem's judgement on the craft, laid on it while the craft is still working perfectly. The last line hangs a single alas at its end to serve both halves, suas and nati: one word does for his own wings and his son's, and the sentence will not separate them.

sentences.t:
Hos aliquis tremula dum captat harundine pisces,
aut pastor baculo stivave innixus arator
vidit et obstipuit, quique aethera carpere possent
credidit esse deos.
sentences.l: These, someone catching fish with a quivering rod, or a shepherd leaning on his staff, or a ploughman on his plough-handle, saw and was struck dumb, and believed them to be gods, seeing that they could make their way through the upper air.
sentences.i: Somebody fishing with a trembling rod, or a shepherd leaning on his crook, or a ploughman on his plough-tail, saw them and stood amazed, and took them for gods, since they could travel the open sky.
sentences.n: Three watchers and one verb: aliquis, pastor and arator are all subjects of the singular vidit and obstipuit, which is normal in Latin when the subjects are alternatives rather than a group. The -que of quique is a connective joining credidit to vidit, pushed back onto the relative pronoun, a habit of verse. possent is subjunctive in a causal relative clause: they must be gods, seeing that they can do this. carpere viam is the ordinary Latin for making one's way — carpe viam was Daedalus's own word at line 208 — and here it is the upper air that is being taken.

sentences.t:
Et iam Iunonia laeva
parte Samos (fuerant Delosque Parosque relictae),
dextra Lebinthos erat fecundaque melle Calymne,
sentences.l: And already Juno's Samos was on the left side (Delos and Paros had been left behind), on the right was Lebinthos, and Calymne fruitful with honey,
sentences.i: By now Juno's Samos lay on the left — Delos and Paros were already behind them — and on the right Lebinthos, and Calymne rich in honey,
sentences.n: Iunonia Samos: the island was Juno's, and the adjective is doing the work of a genitive, which Latin prefers with places. The five names are a flight-path — what is passed, what is to the left, what is to the right — and the reader is meant to see the two of them moving. relictae is feminine plural agreeing with the two island names, and the pluperfect fuerant relictae sets them further back in time than the rest of the sentence. erat is singular and serves Lebinthos and Calymne both. melle is ablative with fecunda, “fruitful in honey”.

sentences.t:
cum puer audaci coepit gaudere volatu
deseruitque ducem caelique cupidine tractus
altius egit iter.
sentences.l: when the boy began to take pleasure in the bold flight, and deserted his leader, and, drawn by a longing for the sky, drove his road higher.
sentences.i: when the boy began to enjoy the daring of it, and left his guide behind, and, pulled by a craving for the sky, took his course higher.
sentences.n: This is the inverted cum construction: the long sentence about islands to left and right is only the setting, and the cum-clause carries the event, so the weight of the whole period falls at its end. ducem picks up me duce from the warning at line 208 — the boy leaves behind exactly the thing he was told to follow. caeli cupidine is an objective genitive, “desire for the sky”. altius is a comparative adverb used absolutely, “higher than he should”, the same use as demissior and celsior in the warning.

sentences.t:
Rapidi vicinia solis
mollit odoratas, pennarum vincula, ceras.
sentences.l: The nearness of the scorching sun softens the fragrant wax, the bonds of the feathers.
sentences.i: The nearness of the burning sun softened the sweet-smelling wax that bound the feathers.
sentences.n: rapidus of the sun is not “swift” but “snatching, consuming” — the root is rapio, and it is the heat that seizes. odoratas is beeswax, which smells, and the adjective is doing work rather than decorating: it is the same wax the boy was softening under his thumb while playing at lines 198-199. pennarum vincula stands in apposition between the adjective and its noun, so the wax is named as fragrant, then named again as the thing that holds the wing together, and only then does the word ceras arrive.

sentences.t:
Tabuerant cerae: nudos quatit ille lacertos,
remigioque carens non ullas percipit auras,
sentences.l: The waxes had melted away: he shakes bare arms and, lacking his oarage, gets hold of no air at all.
sentences.i: The wax was gone. He beat bare arms, and with nothing left to row with there was no air for him to take hold of.
sentences.n: tabuerant is pluperfect: the melting is already finished before the line begins, which is why there is nothing left to describe. remigium is a ship's oarage, the whole gear of rowing, and it is the poem's word for the wings. non ullas is the emphatic form and is stronger than nullas: not any air at all. quatit is a historic present set hard against the pluperfect, and that switch is what makes the fall sudden.

sentences.t:
oraque caerulea patrium clamantia nomen
excipiuntur aqua: quae nomen traxit ab illo.
sentences.l: and the mouth calling his father's name is caught by the dark-blue water: which drew its name from him.
sentences.i: and the mouth calling out his father's name was taken by the blue water, and the water drew its name from him.
sentences.n: ora is a neuter plural used of a single mouth, which is normal in verse, and clamantia agrees with it. patrium nomen is “the father's name”, the word a boy cries; in the lines that follow the father cries the boy's name back at him three times. excipiuntur is passive, “are caught, are received” — excipio is the verb for catching a thing as it falls, so the water is what does the taking and the boy is what is taken. quae is a connecting relative attached to aqua, “and it”. The naming arrives in the same breath as the death: nomen ends the boy's line and stands again in the middle of the sea's.

sentences.t:
At pater infelix, nec iam pater, “Icare,” dixit,
“Icare,” dixit “ubi es? qua te regione requiram?”
“Icare” dicebat:
sentences.l: But the unhappy father, and now not a father, said, “Icarus,” said “Icarus, where are you? In what quarter am I to look for you?” “Icarus,” he kept saying:
sentences.i: But the unhappy father — no longer a father — said “Icarus.” He said, “Icarus, where are you? What quarter am I to search for you in?” “Icarus,” he went on saying.
sentences.n: nec iam pater is three words that undo the word before them: he is called father and unfathered in one breath. The name is said three times and the verb changes under it — dixit, dixit, and then the imperfect dicebat, which turns two finished cries into a calling that does not stop. The flatness of the repeated dixit is the effect and is kept. requiram is a deliberative subjunctive, “where am I to look for you?”, a question that expects no answer; qua regione is ablative, “in what quarter”.

sentences.t:
pennas adspexit in undis
devovitque suas artes corpusque sepulcro
condidit, et tellus a nomine dicta sepulti.
sentences.l: he caught sight of feathers on the waves, and cursed his own arts, and laid the body away in a tomb, and the land was named from the name of the one buried.
sentences.i: he saw feathers on the water, and cursed the skill that was his own, and buried the body in a tomb, and the land was called after the name of the boy laid in it.
sentences.n: devovere is stronger than regretting: it is to curse a thing, to hand it over to the powers below. suas is emphatic — the arts are his own, and it is his own that he curses. dicta stands without est, which verse allows and does constantly. sepulti is a perfect participle used as a noun, “of the one buried”, and the boy's name is not written here: it has just been said three times over and now it belongs to a place.

sentences.t:
Hunc miseri tumulo ponentem corpora nati
garrula limoso prospexit ab elice perdix
et plausit pennis testataque gaudia cantu est:
sentences.l: Him, as he was laying the body of his wretched son in the tomb, a chattering partridge watched from a muddy ditch, and clapped with her wings, and gave witness of her joy in song:
sentences.i: As he laid the body of his poor son in the grave, a chattering partridge watched him from a muddy ditch, and clapped her wings, and testified her delight with a song:
sentences.n: corpora is a poetic plural for one body. miseri agrees with nati, not with Hunc: it is the son who is called wretched, though the father is the one standing at the grave. elix is a drainage furrow cut across a field, a low wet place, and the bird's position matters — the last lines of this part say why. testata … est is the perfect of testor, a deponent — passive in form, active in meaning, “she bore witness”. The bird's joy is given here with no explanation, and the reason is held back for three lines.

sentences.t:
unica tunc volucris nec visa prioribus annis,
factaque nuper avis, longum tibi, Daedale, crimen.
sentences.l: at that time the one bird of her kind, and not seen in earlier years, and lately made a bird — a long charge against you, Daedalus.
sentences.i: the only one of her kind then, unseen in earlier years, newly made a bird: a standing charge against you, Daedalus.
sentences.n: This is an apostrophe: the poem turns aside from the story and speaks to Daedalus directly, tibi, Daedale, with the vocative landing in the middle of the line. crimen is the accusation, the thing charged, not the deed — so the bird itself is the charge, alive and out in the open where he can see it — and longum makes the charge lasting rather than lengthy. unica is one of a kind, not merely one: there had been no partridge in the world before.

sentences.t:
Namque huic tradiderat, fatorum ignara, docendam
progeniem germana suam, natalibus actis
bis puerum senis, animi ad praecepta capacis.
sentences.l: For to him his sister had handed over her own offspring to be taught, not knowing the fates — a boy with twice six birthdays completed, of a mind able to take instruction.
sentences.i: For his sister had put her own child into his hands to be taught, with no notion of what the fates held: a boy of twelve years, with a mind that could take what it was given.
sentences.n: docendam is a gerundive agreeing with progeniem, “to be taught”, which is the ordinary way Latin expresses purpose after a verb of handing over. fatorum ignara is feminine and agrees with germana: it is the sister who does not know. natalibus actis bis senis is an ablative absolute, “with twice six birthdays completed”, and bis senis for twelve is verse arithmetic — verse dislikes plain numerals. animi … capacis is a genitive of quality describing the boy, and capax with ad is “roomy enough for, able to hold”.

sentences.t:
Ille etiam medio spinas in pisce notatas
traxit in exemplum ferroque incidit acuto
perpetuos dentes et serrae repperit usum.
sentences.l: He too took the spines he had noticed in the middle of a fish as a model, and cut a continuous row of teeth in sharp iron, and found out the use of the saw.
sentences.i: It was he who took the ridge of bone he had noticed inside a fish for a model, cut an unbroken row of teeth into sharp iron, and so discovered the saw.
sentences.n: traxit in exemplum is “drew into a pattern”, the Latin idiom for taking a thing as a model. notatas is a perfect participle agreeing with spinas, “marked, noticed”. perpetuus is unbroken and continuous, and a row of teeth running the whole length is exactly what makes a saw a saw. medio in pisce is “in the middle of the fish”, not “in a middle fish”: medius agreeing with a noun means the middle part of that noun, which is how Latin ordinarily says “the middle of”.

sentences.t:
Primus et ex uno duo ferrea bracchia nodo
vinxit, ut aequali spatio distantibus illis
altera pars staret, pars altera duceret orbem.
sentences.l: He was the first, too, to bind two iron arms out of a single joint, so that, with them standing apart at an equal interval, the one part might stand still and the other part draw a circle.
sentences.i: He was the first as well to fasten two iron arms at a single joint, so that with the pair held a fixed distance apart, one leg could stand still and the other trace a circle.
sentences.n: Primus is a nominative adjective used predicatively — “he first bound” — which is how Latin names an inventor, with the adjective and not an adverb. nodus is the knot or joint where the two legs are pinned. aequali spatio distantibus illis is an ablative absolute, “with them standing apart by an equal space”. altera … altera is the pair-word, one of two and then the other, and Ovid reverses the order the second time, altera pars and then pars altera, so that the phrase opens and closes as the instrument does. The thing described is a pair of compasses, and the poem never names it.

sentences.t:
Daedalus invidit sacraque ex arce Minervae
praecipitem misit, lapsum mentitus.
sentences.l: Daedalus envied him, and from the sacred citadel of Minerva sent him headlong, feigning a fall.
sentences.i: Daedalus was envious, and threw him headlong from Minerva's sacred citadel, and lied that he had fallen.
sentences.n: invidit is used here with no object expressed; the person envied is the boy of the last two units, and Latin lets the dative go unsaid where the sense is plain. praecipitem is an adjective agreeing with the boy, “headlong”, where English wants an adverb: Latin puts the manner into the person. mentitus is the perfect participle of mentior, a deponent — passive in form, active in meaning, “having lied” — and lapsum is the accusative of the noun lapsus, “a fall”, the thing he lied about. The murder takes a line and a half; the lie takes two words.

sentences.t:
At illum
quae favet ingeniis excepit Pallas avemque
reddidit et medio velavit in aere pennis.
sentences.l: But him, Pallas, who favours talents, caught, and gave him back as a bird, and in mid-air clothed him with feathers.
sentences.i: But Pallas, who is on the side of the gifted, caught him, and gave him back as a bird, and feathered him over in mid-air.
sentences.n: The relative clause quae favet ingeniis comes before its antecedent Pallas, so the reason for the rescue is given before the name of the rescuer. excepit is the same verb that took Icarus at line 230: there the sea caught a falling boy, here a goddess catches one, and the two falls answer each other. ingeniis is dative after favet, and ingenium is native talent, the thing this boy had just been shown to have. velavit, “veiled, covered over”, is a clothing word: the feathers arrive on him as a garment.

sentences.t:
Sed vigor ingenii quondam velocis in alas
inque pedes abiit: nomen quod et ante remansit.
sentences.l: But the force of his once-swift talent went off into his wings and into his feet: the name which he had before also remained.
sentences.i: But the quickness that had been in his mind passed into his wings and his feet: the name he had before stayed with him too.
sentences.n: quondam here means “formerly”, of the boy's living wit — not the “at times” it meant in the pipe simile earlier in this part, and the two uses are worth setting side by side. vigor ingenii … in alas abiit states the transformation as a transfer: what was quickness of mind becomes quickness of body, with nothing added and nothing lost. et here is “also”, not “and”. The name that stays is perdix, which is the word for the partridge, so the bird's name and the boy's are one word.

sentences.t:
Non tamen haec alte volucris sua corpora tollit,
nec facit in ramis altoque cacumine nidos:
sentences.l: Yet this bird does not lift her body high, nor make her nests in branches and on a high treetop:
sentences.i: All the same, this bird does not carry herself high, and does not build in the branches or on the high crown of a tree:
sentences.n: corpora is again a poetic plural for one body, as at line 236. tamen sets the whole sentence against the transformation just described: she has been given wings and does not use them upward. altoque cacumine is an ablative of place with no preposition, which verse allows freely; cacumen is the topmost point of a tree.

sentences.t:
propter humum volitat ponitque in saepibus ova
antiquique memor metuit sublimia casus.
sentences.l: she flits close to the ground, and lays her eggs in hedgerows, and, remembering the old fall, she fears high places.
sentences.i: she flutters low along the ground, and lays her eggs in the hedges, and, with that old fall in her memory, is afraid of anything high.
sentences.n: propter here is the preposition “near, close by”, not the causal “on account of”; the two are the same word and only the sense decides which is meant. memor takes a genitive, antiqui casus, “mindful of the old fall”. casus is both the fall from the citadel and the disaster, and the word carries both at once. sublimia is a neuter plural adjective used as a noun, “the high places”. The last word of the tale is casus, and the last thing the bird does is remember.
